b: Acute gastritis involves inflammation without mucosal injury (e.g., NSAIDs, alcohol, stress); severe cases can lead to acute haemorrhagic erosive gastropathy . Chronic gastritis is characterized by mucosal inflammation, atrophy, and metapla

H. pylori Gastritis: This is the most common chronic gastritis, predominantly affects the antrum , is associated with increased acid secretion, and can lead to PUD , MALT lymphoma , and adenocarcinoma .

Autoimmune Gastritis: This affects the body and fundus , is associated with anti-parietal cell and anti-intrinsic factor antibodies , leading to achlorhydria (decreased acid) and hypergastrinemia . It is a major cause of pernicious anaemia

qs.q: A patient is diagnosed with a gastric MALT lymphoma driven by chronic gastritis. Which of the following infectious agents is primarily implicated in the pathogenesis and potential regression of this early-stage tumour upon eradication?
qs.e: Gastric MALT lymphoma is derived from mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue induced by chronic Helicobacter pylori gastritis, and eradication of this bacterium can lead to tumour regression.
qs.s: Tumours of the Gastrointestinal Tract — Notes: MCQs

qs.q: What is the deepest layer of the gastric wall involved in true gastritis based on standard definitions?
qs.e: Gastritis is defined as inflammation of the gastric mucosa with sparing of the muscularis mucosa. The lamina propria is part of the mucosa and gets involved, unlike the deeper layers.

qs.q: Which form of chronic gastritis specifically involves the fundus and body of the stomach and is primarily autoimmune-mediated?
qs.e: Type A gastritis predominantly involves the fundus and body and is autoimmune-mediated, often associated with pernicious anaemia. Type B gastritis is antrum-dominant and linked to H. pylori.

qs.q: What is the primary histological hallmark used to differentiate chronic gastritis from acute gastritis on a biopsy sample?
o: Presence of lymphocytes and plasma cells with scanty neutrophils
Dense sheets of eosinophils within the superficial layers
Prominent mucosal neutrophilic infiltration with marked oedema
Total absence of inflammatory cells with complete glandular loss
qs.e: Chronic gastritis is identified by the presence of lymphocytes and plasma cells with scanty neutrophils. Neutrophils dominate in acute gastritis.

qs.q: A patient with chronic gastritis is found to have inflammation extending deeper into the mucosa with distortion and destruction of the gastric glands. What is this classification called?
qs.e: Atrophic gastritis features inflammation extending deeper into the mucosa with distortion and destruction of the glands. Superficial chronic gastritis keeps inflammatory changes limited to the lamina propria.

qs.q: In the management of low grade B cell MALT lymphoma associated with chronic gastritis, what is the primary targeted treatment approach?
qs.e: H. pylori infection is associated with low grade B cell MALT lymphoma, and treatment of MALT is achieved by eradicating the H. pylori infection. Glucocorticoids are used for eosinophilic gastritis.

qs.q: Which specific variant of gastritis is characterized by clinical atopy and marked infiltration of superficial layers by a specific granulocyte, responding well to glucocorticoids?
qs.e: Eosinophilic gastritis involves marked eosinophilic infiltration of superficial layers and is seen in patients with clinical atopy, treated with glucocorticoids. Lymphocytic gastritis has unknown etiology with no significant H. pylori role.

qs.q: During the diagnostic workup for chronic gastritis, from which anatomical regions of the stomach should multiple histological tissue samples ideally be taken?
qs.e: Endoscopy for chronic gastritis involves taking multiple tissue samples from suspicious looking areas, preferably from the fundus, body and antrum. Sampling only the antrum misses fundal-predominant lesions.

ai.summary: Gastritis is inflammation of the gastric mucosa that can be acute or chronic. In East Africa, infections, medications, and nutritional factors dominate. Clinical reasoning focuses on history, bedside signs, and pragmatic investigations.

sections.p: Gastritis is mucosal inflammation of the stomach lining. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by simple tests when available. In low‑resource settings, a focused history and bedside examination guide management.
b: Acute: sudden epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, possible haematemesis or melena
Chronic: dull epigastric discomfort, early satiety, weight loss

t.b: Is anaemia present? Low Hb suggests chronic blood loss or malnutrition
Is thrombocytopenia present? May indicate portal hypertension or bone marrow suppression
Detects H. pylori. Positive suggests chronic gastritis; negative does not rule it out if symptoms persist
Gold standard for ulcer, malignancy, or severe erosions; used when available and patient is unstable

sections.p: Severity is graded by clinical features and endoscopic findings. In practice, we use a simple three‑tier system: mild, moderate, severe.
b: Mild: pain only, no bleeding, normal vitals
Moderate: pain with vomiting, mild tachycardia, possible occult blood
Severe: haematemesis, melena, hypotension, tachycardia, or shock

t.b: Assess haemodynamic stability; hypotension or tachycardia indicates severe bleeding

sections.p: Etiology is grouped by exposure, infection, medication, and systemic disease. In East Africa, infections and herbal remedies are common.
b: Infections: H. pylori (most common chronic), malaria (stress gastritis), HIV (immune dysregulation)
Medications: NSAIDs, aspirin, antimalarials, antiretrovirals, psychotropics
Alcohol and tobacco
Herbal preparations (e.g., Kigelia, miso), over‑the‑counter remedies
Stress in critical illness (ICU, burns)
Autoimmune (rare)

t.b: Non‑invasive detection of infection; positive supports chronic gastritis
Elevated in autoimmune gastritis; low in H. pylori

sections.p: Presentation varies with acuity. Bedside clues guide urgency.
b: Chronic: dull epigastric discomfort, early satiety, weight loss, occasional nausea

t.b: Look for epigastric tenderness, guarding, rebound; absence of peritonitis suggests non‑perforated gastritis

sections.p: Use tests that are affordable and available. Prioritise those that change management.
b: Stool occult blood
Basic metabolic panel

t.b: Detects anaemia or leukocytosis; anaemia suggests chronic bleeding or malnutrition
Positive indicates H. pylori; treat with antibiotics
Positive supports bleeding; negative does not exclude intermittent bleeding
Assess electrolytes; hypokalaemia may worsen arrhythmias in severe vomiting

sections.p: Certain signs warrant immediate transfer or intervention.
b: Melena with hypotension
Persistent vomiting > 48 h
Severe epigastric pain with guarding
Signs of shock (tachycardia >120, capillary refill >2 s)

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, provide supportive care, and monitor closely.
b: Refer to higher centre if perforation or uncontrolled bleeding suspected

t.b: Reduces acid, promotes healing, and decreases bleeding risk
Stabilises clots; used when bleeding is uncontrolled and no contraindication

sections.p: After acute episode, reassess and prevent recurrence.

faq.q: What is the first step in managing a patient with suspected acute gastritis?
faq.a: Stop any offending drugs, give a proton pump inhibitor, and assess haemodynamic stability.

faq.q: Why is a proton pump inhibitor preferred over H2 blockers in acute gastritis?
faq.a: PPIs provide stronger acid suppression and faster symptom relief, reducing bleeding risk.

faq.q: How do you treat H. pylori in a setting without culture facilities?
faq.a: Use a standard triple therapy regimen (PPI + clarithromycin + amoxicillin) if local resistance is low, otherwise use bismuth quadruple therapy.

exam: What is the most likely cause of acute epigastric pain with haematemesis in a patient on NSAIDs? — NSAID‑induced erosive gastritis; explain pathophysiology and immediate management steps.

A patient presents with dull epigastric discomfort, early satiety, and weight loss. What is the most likely diagnosis and first investigation? — Chronic gastritis, likely H. pylori; first test is rapid urease test.
During a ward round you find a patient with melena and hypotension. What is the next step? — Immediate resuscitation with IV fluids, blood transfusion if needed, and urgent endoscopy if available.
Why is tranexamic acid contraindicated in a patient with a history of thromboembolism? — It stabilises clots and increases risk of thrombosis.
A patient on chronic antipsychotics develops epigastric pain. Which drug class should be avoided and why? — NSAIDs/aspirin; they increase gastric mucosal damage.
Explain how autoimmune gastritis leads to pernicious anaemia. — Loss of parietal cells → achlorhydria → impaired B12 absorption → macrocytic anaemia.

In a resource‑limited setting, how would you differentiate gastritis from peptic ulcer disease based on bedside findings? — Look for pain relief with food (PUD) vs pain with NSAIDs/alcohol (gastritis).
